::: {.lesson-kicker}
WEEK 1 · REPRESENTATION, RULES, AND SHARED DATA
:::

# A database is just a glorified spreadsheet.

That claim is useful precisely because it is almost plausible. Spreadsheets, CSV files, and database tables can all put values into rows and columns. The real question is not what they look like. The real question is what kinds of work they support reliably.

::: {.lesson-question}
**Guiding question:** When does a simple table stop being "good enough," and what problem is a database actually solving?
:::
:::

## Learning goals

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

1. explain why spreadsheets, CSV files, and database tables initially look similar;
2. distinguish a file or spreadsheet from a database system used for shared structured data;
3. identify repeated information, hidden assumptions, and common inconsistency risks in a naive table;
4. explain why identity, relationships, and rules are hard to maintain in an ordinary file; and
5. choose a spreadsheet, a collection of files, or a database for a small scenario and defend the choice.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Keep one sentence in mind

A database is valuable not merely because it stores data, but because it helps make important **information, rules, and relationships explicit**.
:::

## 1. Why the comparison feels reasonable

Imagine receiving this file from a field team monitoring stream temperature.

| observation_id | site_code | site_name | sensor_model | observed_at | temperature_c |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---:|
| 1 | CC-01 | Clear Creek | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 09:00 | 8.4 |
| 2 | CC-01 | Clear Creek | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 10:00 | 9.1 |
| 3 | PR-02 | Pine River | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 09:00 | 7.8 |
| 4 | CC-01 | Clear Creak | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 11:00 | 9.7 |

At first glance, the same information could live in several places:

::: {.tool-comparison}
::: {.tool-card}
### Spreadsheet

A visible grid with formulas, charts, formatting, and direct editing.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### CSV file

A portable text file that stores rows and delimited values.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### Database table

Rows and columns managed by software designed for shared structured data.
:::
:::

They share a familiar surface:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Rows"] --> D["Tabular data"]
    B["Columns"] --> D
    C["Values"] --> D
    D --> E["Spreadsheet"]
    D --> F["CSV file"]
    D --> G["Database table"]

    classDef shared fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d,stroke-width:1.5px;
    classDef tool fill:#ffffff,stroke:#78909c,color:#21313a;
    class A,B,C,D shared;
    class E,F,G tool;
```

This is why the comparison feels reasonable. For small tasks, the tools may even behave similarly.

### What all three can do

- Store rectangular data.
- Label fields with column names.
- Let a person inspect values directly.
- Support sorting, filtering, and simple summarizing.
- Move data from one tool to another.

::: {.opening-prompt}
## Opening Question

If this file contains only a few hundred rows and one person maintains it, what problem would a database solve today? "Probably none yet" is a legitimate answer.
:::

## 2. A simple table can fail in predictable ways

The core issue is not that rows and columns are bad. The core issue is that a naive table often tries to do several jobs at once.

In this example, one file is trying to:

- record individual observations;
- describe sites;
- describe sensors; and
- carry rules that readers are expected to remember.

That creates several predictable failure patterns.

| Failure pattern | Central question |
|---|---|
| Repeated information | What information is being copied across many rows? |
| Inferred but unenforced rules | What does a human assume that the file does not guarantee? |
| Slippery identity | How do we tell whether two rows refer to the same thing? |
| Awkward relationships | What structure does one wide table hide poorly? |
| Shared editing | What happens when several people change the same data? |

## 3. Failure pattern 1: repeated information invites inconsistent edits

Return to the stream table. Each row looks like one record, but it actually mixes information about several different things.

::: {.fact-grid}
::: {.fact-card}
### Observation information

- when the reading happened
- what temperature was recorded
:::

::: {.fact-card}
### Site information

- the site code
- the site name
:::

::: {.fact-card}
### Sensor information

- the sensor model
- perhaps other details not shown here
:::
:::

The file stores that information together because that is convenient for reading one row. But convenience has a cost: some information now repeats every time a new observation is added.

::: {.tool-comparison}
::: {.tool-card}
### What repeats

Information about sites and sensors is copied into many observation rows.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### What can go wrong

One copy is edited while another is not, so the file starts making contradictory claims.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### Why it matters

The problem is not one typo. The problem is a structure that makes contradiction easy.
:::
:::

The problem is not simply that a value appears more than once. The problem is that the same information about the same thing appears in many rows.

For example:

- "`CC-01` refers to Clear Creek" is information about a site.
- "`TempCo T100` is the sensor model used here" is information about a sensor.

That information is copied again and again as more observations are recorded.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Row 4 is not merely a typo

`CC-01` now appears with both `Clear Creek` and `Clear Creak`. The visible mistake matters, but the design issue matters more: the file makes it easy for the same site information to be copied inconsistently.
:::

### A small inconsistency can spread

Suppose the site name changes, or the original name was misspelled.

| Task | Risk in one flat file |
|---|---|
| Correct the site name | Some rows get updated and others do not |
| Add a new site before its first reading | You may be forced to invent a fake reading or leave the site out entirely |
| Delete the final reading from a site | You may also delete the only remaining record of the site |

You do not need formal vocabulary yet to see the pattern: when one file mixes several kinds of information, ordinary edits become risky.

::: {.activity-checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** Which information in the table is about one reading, and which information is about something that exists across many readings?
:::

## 4. Failure pattern 2: human readers infer rules the file does not enforce

A human reader naturally makes inferences from the table:

- that `CC-01` identifies one site;
- that `site_name` should be consistent for that site;
- that every observation came from a real site;
- that `2026-05-01 09:00` is intended to be a date-time value;
- that temperature should be numeric and within some plausible range.

Some of those assumptions may be reasonable. But notice that the file itself does not explain which are guaranteed and which are merely guesses.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## People can carry rules that the file cannot

Humans can look at a column and think, "those are timestamps," or "those codes should be unique." A plain file does not automatically enforce either claim.
:::

::: {.tool-comparison}
::: {.tool-card}
### What people infer

Certain columns "should" be unique, numeric, or date-like.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### What the file knows

Usually much less than the reader assumes.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### Why it matters

Data can look meaningful and still fail to preserve that meaning reliably.
:::
:::

### A table can suggest structure without enforcing it

Consider the values below:

| Column | What a person may infer | What the file itself guarantees |
|---|---|---|
| `site_code` | One code per site | Very little by itself |
| `observed_at` | A date and time | Only that some text was stored |
| `temperature_c` | A numeric Celsius value | Only that a value was entered |

This is one reason data integrity is hard in a naive representation. The meaning may be clear to a person and still be fragile in the data itself.

## 5. Failure pattern 3: identity becomes slippery

When a table is small, people often act as if labels are identities. That works until labels change, collide, or are entered differently by different people.

Consider the phrase "the Clear Creek site." What exactly identifies it?

- The name is readable, but names can change or be typed inconsistently.
- The code looks stable, but only if the organization treats it as stable.
- The row number identifies a row in this file, not necessarily the real-world site.

The practical issue is simple: if you do not decide how something is identified, you will eventually struggle to tell whether two rows refer to the same thing.

::: {.tool-comparison}
::: {.tool-card}
### The tempting shortcut

Treat the most readable label as the identifier.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### The risk

Readable labels can change, collide, or be entered inconsistently.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### Why it matters

Once identity is unclear, correction, merging, and querying all become harder.
:::
:::

### Questions worth asking early

Before relying on a field as an identifier, ask:

1. Can the value change?
2. Can two real things legitimately share it?
3. Can it be missing?
4. Is it controlled carefully, or typed freely by many people?
5. Does it identify the thing itself, or only one row in one file?

::: {.callout-question appearance="simple"}
## Interpret the evidence

Does `site_code` look more stable than `site_name` here? Why might that still be only an inference rather than a guarantee?
:::

## 6. Failure pattern 4: relationships fit awkwardly into one wide table

Flat tables are good at listing rows. They are less good at representing more complicated relationships.

Suppose one observation can have several quality flags:

- `suspected_ice`
- `sensor_recalibrated`
- `manually_reviewed`

Several file-based designs are tempting:

```text
flag_1 | flag_2 | flag_3
```

```text
flags = "suspected_ice; manually_reviewed"
```

```text
suspected_ice | sensor_recalibrated | manually_reviewed
```

Each choice solves one short-term problem while creating new long-term ones.

- How do we add a new flag type later?
- How do we prevent misspellings?
- How do we record who added a flag and when?
- How do we ask for observations that have two specific flags?

::: {.tool-comparison}
::: {.tool-card}
### The shortcut

Pack relationship information into extra columns or encoded text.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### The risk

New cases become awkward, inconsistent, or hard to query.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### Why it matters

The file hides structure instead of representing it directly.
:::
:::

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    O["One observation"] --> F1["suspected_ice"]
    O --> F2["sensor_recalibrated"]
    O --> F3["manually_reviewed"]
    F1 --> O2["Many observations<br/>can share a flag type"]
    F2 --> O2
    F3 --> O2

    classDef observation fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#ffffff;
    classDef flag fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    class O,O2 observation;
    class F1,F2,F3 flag;
```

The main point is not that spreadsheets are bad. The point is that some relationships fit awkwardly into one rectangular file.

## 7. Why databases help with these failure patterns

A spreadsheet can hint at rules through formatting, protected cells, validation menus, or written instructions. A CSV cannot even do that. In both cases, another person or program may still enter values that break the intended structure.

For the stream data, plausible rules include:

- every observation should refer to a real site;
- a site code should not mean two different sites;
- every observation should have a time;
- temperature should stay in a defensible range;
- two rows should not accidentally describe the same observation event.

You do not need formal syntax yet to see the issue. If a rule matters, relying on memory and careful typing may not be enough.

### A database changes the job of the software

A file mostly stores values.

A database system can do more:

- reject some invalid changes;
- keep related pieces of data consistent;
- coordinate changes from multiple people;
- recover from some failures; and
- answer many different questions over the same stored data.

That is why a database is not just a bigger file. The software is participating in the management of the data, not merely holding it.

## 8. Failure pattern 5: shared editing creates coordination problems

Many file-based workflows handle collaboration by creating copies:

```text
observations.csv
observations_jake_edits.csv
observations_final.csv
observations_final_v2_really_final.csv
```

Copies solve one problem and create another: which file is authoritative?

Even shared spreadsheets can produce subtler conflicts. Two people may each make a reasonable change based on what they saw, yet the combined result may be inconsistent.

::: {.tool-comparison}
::: {.tool-card}
### What each person sees

A plausible local picture of the data.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### What can go wrong

Independent reasonable edits combine into a bad global state.
:::

::: {.tool-card}
### Why it matters

Shared data needs coordination, not only storage.
:::
:::

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as "Analyst A"
    participant D as "Shared data"
    participant B as "Analyst B"
    A->>D: Read sensor status = available
    B->>D: Read sensor status = available
    A->>D: Assign sensor to Team North
    B->>D: Assign sensor to Team South
    Note over A,B: Both actions looked reasonable<br/>from each person's point of view.
```

The Week 1 point is simple: once data is shared, the problem is not only storage. It is also coordination.

## 9. Questions can outgrow the file

Small files are easy to inspect manually. Over time, the workload often changes:

- combine observations with sites, maintenance, weather, or other files;
- answer different questions for different audiences;
- reproduce an earlier report from a trusted state;
- find a small subset quickly;
- allow many readers while new data keeps arriving.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["One table<br/>one person<br/>occasional edits"] --> B["Repeated facts<br/>several kinds of things"]
    B --> C["Shared editing<br/>and conflicting changes"]
    C --> D["Larger workload<br/>more rules and questions"]

    classDef early fill:#f7f3ea,stroke:#9b7b36,color:#3f321c;
    classDef middle fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    classDef late fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#ffffff;
    class A early;
    class B,C middle;
    class D late;
```

Performance is part of the story, but "databases are for big data" is incomplete. A tiny dataset may deserve a database because the rules matter. A huge dataset may work fine in files if it is written once and analyzed in batches.

## 10. Spreadsheets are not failed databases

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Use the simplest tool that preserves what matters

The point is not to replace every spreadsheet. The point is to recognize when a document-oriented grid no longer matches the problem.
:::

### A spreadsheet may be the better choice when

- one person is exploring or entering a modest amount of data;
- layout, annotation, formulas, and charts are part of the artifact;
- the structure changes frequently;
- inconsistent values are easy to notice and low-risk; or
- the document itself is the product.

### A database becomes attractive when

- several kinds of things and relationships must be tracked together;
- identifiers and important rules must stay reliable;
- many people or applications read and write shared data;
- changes must be coordinated and recoverable; or
- the same data must answer many different questions over time.

### Decision matrix

| Situation | Spreadsheet | CSV/files | Database system |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Quick personal exploration | Strong | Moderate | Possible, often unnecessary |
| Portable data interchange | Weak | Strong | Usually exported |
| Rich manual formatting | Strong | None | Not its purpose |
| Shared rules and relationships | Limited | Weak | Strong |
| Concurrent structured updates | Limited | Weak | Strong |
| Recovery from mistakes or failures | Weak | Weak | Strong |
| Long-lived shared data | Limited | Weak | Strong |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## The boundary is contextual

There is no universal row count at which a spreadsheet "becomes" a database problem. The important questions concern rules, repetition, identity, coordination, risk, and workload, not only size.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Continue to Lab 1

Apply these ideas in [Lab 1 - Make the file fail on purpose](../activities/week-01-file-representation-lab.qmd). Working in a small group, you will identify repeated information, surface hidden assumptions, and sketch a first better representation.
:::

## 11. What changed when we moved toward a database?

We did not merely split one file into smaller pieces. We changed what the data system is expected to preserve.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A["A convenient grid"] --> B["Notice repeated information"]
    B --> C["Ask what identifies things"]
    C --> D["Ask which relationships matter"]
    D --> E["Ask which rules must hold"]
    E --> F["Ask how shared changes stay trustworthy"]
    F --> G["A more defensible data system"]

    classDef start fill:#f7f3ea,stroke:#9b7b36,color:#3f321c;
    classDef process fill:#eaf4f7,stroke:#247487,color:#173b4d;
    classDef finish fill:#173b4d,stroke:#173b4d,color:#ffffff;
    class A start;
    class B,C,D,E,F process;
    class G finish;
```

::: {.takeaway-panel}
## The revised claim

A database may look like a collection of tables, but its real value is that it helps preserve meaning, rules, and coordination in data that must be shared and trusted.
:::

## Looking ahead

Next, we will build a more precise vocabulary for talking about data: relation, tuple, attribute, schema, keys, and the difference between a displayed table and the underlying structure it represents.
